# SK0241 — The modifier has no effect

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A keyword that restates what the enclosing declaration has already said: `abstract` on an interface member, `sealed` inside a `sealed` type, `class` after `record`, `: int` on an enum, `readonly` inside a `readonly struct`, `scoped` on an `out` parameter.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Cleanup |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Syntax |
| Needs a compilation | no |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `RedundantAbstractModifier` (`resharper_redundant_abstract_modifier_highlighting`) |
| Supersedes | SealedMemberInSealedClass, RedundantRecordClassKeyword, EnumUnderlyingTypeIsInt, RedundantReadonlyModifier, RedundantScopedParameterModifier |

## Why

A modifier that does nothing is worse than noise, because a reader cannot tell it from one that does. `sealed` on a member of a `sealed` class invites the question of which derived type was going to override it, and there is none; `abstract` on an interface member suggests the interface has members that are not; `readonly` on one member of a `readonly struct` suggests the others are mutable. Each one is answered by a keyword written a few lines above it, and deleting it makes the declaration say exactly what it meant.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
public sealed class Writer : Stream {
    public sealed override void Flush() { }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
public sealed class Writer : Stream {
    public override void Flush() { }
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **`static` withdraws the interface half entirely, and getting it wrong would have been this rule's worst false positive.** A static interface member is *not* implicitly abstract: C# 11's `static abstract T operator +(T, T)` is an abstract static member, and the same declaration without the keyword is a static member that must have a body. Deleting `abstract` there does not tidy anything — it produces a declaration that no longer compiles. ⚠ **A nested type is never the subject.** A type declared inside an interface is not implicitly abstract, and a type nested in a `sealed` class is not implicitly sealed, so the modifier there is the author's; no type declaration is registered as a candidate. ⚠ **A field inside a `readonly struct` is excluded and that is not an oversight.** CS8340 requires every instance field of one to be `readonly`, so the keyword is the language's rather than the author's and deleting it is an error. ⚠ **`enum E : Int32` is left alone.** The rule matches the `int` keyword only, because it has no semantic model to ask what an identifier resolves to and `Int32` is an ordinary identifier that a using directive or a user type can point somewhere else; the keyword cannot be aliased or shadowed, which is what makes matching it exact. ⚠ **A comment or a directive in the keyword's trailing trivia withdraws the finding.** The fix deletes from the keyword to the next token so that a leading documentation comment and attribute list survive, and that span carries the trailing trivia with it — `public /* still virtual in the base */ sealed override` would lose the note under a fix marked safe. ⚠ Six of [#129](https://github.com/Rikarin/SKALA/issues/129)'s eleven inspections are **not** covered. `PartialTypeWithSinglePart` and `PartialMethodWithSinglePart` are the high-volume pair and both need to count a symbol's declarations across the whole compilation — which a source generator can add to after the fact, so a repository whose generated part is missing from a loose load would be told to delete a `partial` it needs. `RedundantVirtualModifier`, `RedundantScopedParameterModifier`, `RedundantUnsafeContext` and `RedundantOverflowCheckingContext` each need to know something about a body or a type that is not written in the declaration. ⚠ **`out` is the only implicitly-scoped parameter form, and that was measured rather than reasoned from the name.** Six spellings were put through `jb inspectcode` 2025.2.6 — `scoped out int`, `scoped out` a `ref struct`, `scoped ref` a `ref struct`, `scoped in` a `ref struct`, `scoped` on a by-value `ref struct`, and `scoped ref int` — and ReSharper reported the two `out` forms and nothing else. The others are not redundant: `scoped` on a `ref` or `in` parameter narrows the ref-safe-to-escape of the reference itself, and deleting it lets the reference escape where it previously could not. Each has a negative fixture.
